profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between a university-based education researcher and a multi-academy trust computing coordinator to prepare a spring-term pilot that adapts ScratchMaths-inspired curriculum materials and teacher professional development for three English primary schools. The context is that the trust wants to use findings about teaching algorithmic thinking and the 360° total turn concept with pupils aged 9-11, while keeping the rollout lightweight enough for busy teachers. The agenda is to agree which classes will participate, what the October and January PD will involve, which lesson materials will be used first, what evidence teachers should return, and who will coordinate support across the pilot. The expected outcome is a shared implementation plan with responsibilities, timeline, and a clear sense of what each school will do in the first half-term.

members.name: Dr. Hannah Price
members.expertise: Design research, primary mathematics education, curriculum-based professional development, evaluation of classroom interventions
members.background: Hannah worked on research projects linking programming and mathematics in upper primary classrooms and now helps schools adapt evidence-based materials without losing the key conceptual design principles.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to stay close enough to the original research design that any teacher feedback and pupil work will still be interpretable, but she does not want to sound rigid or academic in front of a school-facing partner.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to a 'PD session', they usually mean the whole support package around it: pre-reading, the live workshop, and a follow-up coaching touchpoint.
A 'pilot in Year 5 and 6' normally means one nominated class per year group in each participating school, because early trials need manageable implementation.
Saying a teacher has 'trialled the algorithm lesson' implies the core Scratch-based lesson sequence was taught in full, even if some classroom discussion was adapted.
When colleagues mention 'the 360° task', they are usually talking about the on-screen sprite-turning activity that anchors the mathematical idea inside Scratch.

members.name: Mark Ellison
members.role: Primary Computing and STEM Coordinator for a Multi-Academy Trust
members.expertise: School implementation planning, teacher CPD logistics, curriculum coordination across primary schools, classroom adoption of computing resources
members.background: Mark was previously a Year 6 teacher and now coordinates computing across six trust schools, translating external projects into workable plans that headteachers and class teachers can actually sustain.
members.private_state: He wants the trust to look ambitious and coherent across schools, while minimizing anything that feels like extra monitoring or dependence on outside researchers.
hidden_assumptions: A 'PD session' is the live event itself; any pre-read or follow-up support is optional enrichment rather than part of the delivery commitment.
If a trust says it is piloting something in 'Year 5 and 6', that ordinarily means all Year 5 and Year 6 classes in the participating schools, so the pilot looks whole-school rather than selective.
A teacher has 'trialled the algorithm lesson' if they have taught the main idea in a way that fits their class, including unplugged or shortened versions before moving into Scratch later.
The phrase 'the 360° task' refers to the printed floor/path activity from the handbook because that is the easiest thing for teachers to run first and the most memorable PD artifact.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the first PD session
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to run 'the first PD session' in October.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means an October PD cycle consisting of advance reading, a 90-minute live workshop, and a short classroom follow-up check-in.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a single 90-minute after-school workshop in October, with anything else treated as optional rather than scheduled delivery.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In school-improvement conversations, 'PD session' is commonly used as shorthand, and both participants are accustomed to bundling or unbundling surrounding activities without explicitly naming the difference.

misalignment_points.topic: Who is included in the Year 5 and 6 pilot
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss piloting the materials 'in Year 5 and 6 across the three schools'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes each school will nominate one Year 5 class and one Year 6 class, keeping the pilot bounded and easier to support.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes every Year 5 and Year 6 class in those schools is included once the trust commits to the pilot.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds completely ordinary and both interpretations are institutionally plausible; because they are planning at a high level, neither feels a need to restate the unit of participation.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to have trialled the algorithm lesson
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree teachers should 'trial the algorithm lesson before half-term'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 takes this to mean teachers teach the intended Scratch-based lesson sequence on algorithms and submit pupil work or notes from that full sequence.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 takes this to mean teachers expose pupils to the algorithm concept in any reasonable local adaptation before half-term, even if they only do an unplugged or shortened version and postpone Scratch.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both support teacher adaptation and use the same success language, so the divergence hides inside their different thresholds for what counts as a completed trial.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They mention starting with 'the 360° task' when sequencing materials.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the Scratch sprite-turning activity designed to help pupils connect repeated turns to a total turn of 360°.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the paper-and-floor movement activity from the PD handbook that teachers often remember as the 360° task.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both activities target the same concept, both are informally labeled with the same phrase, and each participant assumes the other is recalling the most salient version from their own context.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this grounded and practical. If we can adapt the ScratchMaths-inspired work without stripping out the core design ideas, we'll still be able to learn something useful from what teachers do. I want a plan that protects the research logic around algorithms and total turn, but I don't want to sound as though I'm imposing a university model on schools.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time, Mark. I think today is really about landing a practical plan for the spring-term pilot around algorithms and 360° total turn, so we know what the three schools are doing, what support sits around it, and what we'll want back from classrooms.

turns.inner_thought: What I need is something that looks coherent across the trust, not a tiny boutique trial. If we say we're doing this in Year 5 and 6 across the three schools, that means every Year 5 and Year 6 class in those schools. Heads will want to see a proper upper-KS2 offer, and I don't want this to become a heavily researcher-managed exercise.
turns.utterance: Yes, exactly. From the trust side, we'd like this to run in Year 5 and 6 across the three schools, so leaders can see it as a coherent upper-KS2 piece rather than something too isolated.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that sounds workable if each school has one class in Year 5 and one in Year 6. We should get the first PD session in by October, and for me that includes the advance reading, the live workshop, and then a short follow-up touchpoint so teachers don't go into classroom delivery cold.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I think it would help if the first PD session happened in October, just so teachers have enough runway to get familiar with the materials before they start teaching in the spring.

turns.inner_thought: October is fine. A single 90-minute after-school slot is realistic; anything more starts to feel heavy. And if we're bringing in Year 5 and 6 across the three schools, I can get all those teachers there in one go if we pin the date down early.
turns.utterance: Yes, October would work well. We could aim for an after-school slot then, which should be the easiest way to get Year 5 and 6 staff in from all three schools.

turns.inner_thought: If they start with the Scratch-based 360° task, they'll see the mathematical point inside the programming activity from the outset. That gives a strong conceptual anchor and makes later pupil work much more interpretable.
turns.utterance: In terms of sequencing, I'd be inclined to begin with the 360° task, because it gives teachers a really concrete way into linking programming moves with mathematical reasoning.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, the paper-and-floor 360° task is exactly the sort of low-entry activity teachers will actually try first. It feels safe, memorable, and manageable, especially for staff who are less confident with Scratch.
turns.utterance: I agree. The 360° task should land well as a first classroom activity, especially for colleagues who need an accessible starting point.

turns.inner_thought: After that launch piece, I need them to teach the actual Scratch-based algorithm lesson sequence before half-term, not just touch the idea loosely. Otherwise the evidence won't tell us much about how the designed lesson works in classrooms.
turns.utterance: Then I think, once that initial launch is in place, teachers should trial the algorithm lesson before half-term so we can get some early implementation evidence to work from.

turns.inner_thought: That should be fine. As long as teachers can make it fit their classes, they can definitely trial the algorithm lesson before half-term. For some, that may mean a shorter or unplugged version first, and that's still a legitimate trial as far as I'm concerned.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's reasonable. Teachers can trial the algorithm lesson before half-term, and they'll appreciate a bit of flexibility to make it work for their classes.

turns.inner_thought: I'll put together the October pack so they have the pre-reading and the session materials in one place, and I also want a brief follow-up touchpoint after first teaching so we can catch issues while they're fresh. I should phrase it lightly so it doesn't sound burdensome.
turns.utterance: What I can do is prepare the October materials pack, and then build in a brief follow-up touchpoint after the first classroom teaching so staff have a chance to consolidate anything that comes up.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine, as long as the core ask remains the October session and the teaching itself. I'll coordinate all participating teachers in each school, meaning every Year 5 and Year 6 class teacher, and make sure they protect time for the workshop and to trial the algorithm lesson in whatever form fits before half-term.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll coordinate the participating teachers in each school and make sure they've blocked time for the October session and for that first-half-term teaching window.

turns.inner_thought: Once teachers have taught the Scratch 360° task and the full algorithm lesson sequence, I can look across pupil work, screenshots, and teacher notes to shape January around the real sticking points. That should help us preserve fidelity without sounding like surveillance.
turns.utterance: And once the 360° task and the algorithm lesson are underway, I can review examples coming back from classrooms and use that to shape the January PD.

turns.inner_thought: This sounds neat and presentable: one October PD session, a Year 5 and 6 pilot across the three schools, and teachers trialling the algorithm lesson before half-term. That's a strong trust narrative and still light enough to manage.
turns.utterance: Perfect. So we've got an October first PD session, a Year 5 and 6 pilot across the three schools, and an expectation that teachers will trial the algorithm lesson before half-term. I'll take that summary back to heads and start lining people up.
